title: Xero vs QuickBooks vs Zoho Books: Best Cloud Accounting Software for SMEs
description: Compare Xero, QuickBooks Online and Zoho Books for small and medium businesses: features, reporting, multi-currency, tax handling, integrations and who each suits.
lead: Cloud accounting lets you see your numbers from anywhere, share them with your accountant instantly and cut manual entry. Xero, QuickBooks Online and Zoho Books are the three names SMEs ask about most. Here is how they compare.
body:
At a glance

AreaXeroQuickBooks OnlineZoho Books
Best forService and trading SMEs with an accountant involvedSmall businesses wanting a big ecosystem of apps and accountantsBudget-conscious SMEs, especially those already using Zoho apps
Ease of useClean and simpleVery familiar, many tutorialsSimple, with many settings to explore
Multi-currencyAvailable on higher plansAvailable on higher plansSupported
VAT / GST supportStrong for UK and several regionsStrong for US and UK; varies by countryBuilt-in tax support for several Gulf countries and the UK
IntegrationsLarge app marketplaceVery large app marketplaceDeep link to Zoho CRM, Inventory and other Zoho apps
ReportingGood standard reports, customisableGood standard reportsGood standard reports

Plans, prices and country features change often. Always confirm on the vendor's website before you subscribe.

Xero

Xero is popular with accountants for its clean interface, reconciliation workflow and collaboration tools. It suits businesses that want to work closely with their accounting firm.

QuickBooks Online

QuickBooks has the biggest user base and a very large number of connected apps. It works well for small businesses that sell products or services and want invoicing, expenses and reports in one place. Features vary by country, so check what is available in yours.

Zoho Books

Zoho Books is competitive on price and fits naturally if you already use Zoho CRM or Zoho Inventory. It includes VAT features for several Gulf countries, which helps businesses operating in the UAE, Saudi Arabia or Bahrain.

What about Pakistan?

None of these tools is built around Pakistan's FBR and provincial sales tax portals, so you will usually record tax rates manually and file returns separately. Bank feeds for local banks are usually limited, so statements are often imported by file. A good chart of accounts, tax codes and a clear month-end routine matter more than the software brand.

How to choose

  1. Where do you operate? Pick the tool with the best tax support for that country.
  2. Which other systems must it connect with: POS, payroll, CRM, e-commerce?
  3. How many users and how much inventory do you handle?
  4. What does your accountant already use?
  5. Run a free trial using one month of real transactions before you decide.

Moving from Excel? Clean your customer, supplier and opening balance data first. Importing messy spreadsheets simply moves the mess into the cloud.
